name: Dorothy Blum
milestone_by_age_26: In 1944 at age 20, after graduating Brooklyn College, she joined the U.S. Army wartime cryptologic organization and began a career in cryptanalysis that continued into AFSA/NSA.
early_history_summary: Born in New York City in 1924 to Austro-Hungarian immigrant parents; enrolled at Brooklyn College at 16 as a chemistry major, then shifted toward cryptanalysis coursework that led directly into Army SIGINT work in 1944. She remained in U.S. cryptologic agencies after WWII, pioneering early computer methods including pre-public FORTRAN use at NSA.
primary_leverage_engine: Scarce technical depth in cryptanalysis and early computing
secondary_engine: Wartime institutional demand for codebreaking talent
family_context_summary: Born in New York City to Austrian/Hungarian immigrant parents Joseph and Rebecca Toplitzky; limited public detail on family wealth.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented as a cryptanalysis or computing family apprenticeship path.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Brooklyn College early entry, Army cryptanalysis 1944, NSA computing pioneer, wartime SIGINT demand
evidence_summary: Wikipedia, NSA Hall of Honor, Maryland Women's Hall of Fame, and Cryptologic Almanac agree she was born 1924, graduated Brooklyn College, and joined Army cryptologic work in 1944 at ~20. Later NSA leadership (C7 chief 1972; plans/project development 1977) and early FORTRAN use document scarce computing skill in a classified environment. Family domain advantage is not documented; wartime institutional demand and college cryptanalysis coursework are the clearest early accelerators.
starting_point: Born February 21, 1924 in New York City to Austro-Hungarian immigrant parents; entered Brooklyn College at 16 and pivoted from chemistry into cryptanalysis.
current_position: Died October 1, 1980 at age 56; final NSA role included chief of Plans and Project Development in Telecommunications and Computer Services; posthumously inducted into NSA Hall of Honor (2004).

trajectory.event: Enrolled at Brooklyn College as a chemistry major and later took cryptanalysis coursework that redirected her career.
Graduated Brooklyn College and joined the U.S. Army wartime cryptologic organization as a cryptanalyst.
Continued cryptologic/computer work in post-war AFSA/NSA predecessor organizations; married NSA mathematician Joseph Blum.
At NSA in the 1950s tracked emerging computing methods and applied early FORTRAN years before public release.
Became chief of NSA Computer Operations Organization (C7), then the only woman in that management hierarchy.
Appointed chief of Plans and Project Development Organization (T4) in Telecommunications and Computer Services.
Died of cancer; later honored with an internal NSA award in her name and NSA Hall of Honor induction.

name: Hedy Lamarr
milestone_by_age_26: In 1933 at age 18 she starred in Ecstasy, which brought international notoriety; by 1938 at age 23–24 she became a Hollywood star via Algiers under an MGM contract, well before the 1942 frequency-hopping patent at age 27.
early_history_summary: Born Hedwig Kiesler in Vienna in 1914 to a well-to-do Jewish family (father a bank director; mother a pianist). Entered European film as a teen, led Ecstasy at 18, then escaped controlling marriage to arms merchant Friedrich Mandl and reached Hollywood via Louis B. Mayer. Later, with George Antheil, patented a secret communication system (1942) foundational to spread-spectrum ideas, though military adoption came decades later.
family_context_summary: Only child of Emil Kiesler (bank deputy director/director in Vienna) and Gertrud Lichtwitz Kiesler (pianist from upper-class Hungarian-Jewish family); raised with material comfort and cultural access.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father walked her through how machines worked as a child; not a film-industry apprenticeship, but banking/upper-middle-class stability and informal tech curiosity.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Vienna upper-middle-class family, early beauty/screen presence, European film entry, MGM contract, Mandl tech exposure later
evidence_summary: Wikipedia, National WWII Museum, National Inventors Hall of Fame, and women's history biographies confirm 1914 birth, Ecstasy lead at 18 (1933), Hollywood breakthrough with Algiers (1938), and the Lamarr–Antheil frequency-hopping patent issued August 11, 1942 under Hedy Kiesler Markey at age 27. Acting stardom is the clear ≤26 material milestone; inventing recognition came much later (EFF Pioneer Award 1997; National Inventors Hall of Fame 2014).
starting_point: Born November 9, 1914 in Vienna to a bank-executive father and pianist mother in a well-to-do assimilated Jewish family.
current_position: Died January 19, 2000 at age 85 in Casselberry, Florida; remembered as Golden Age film star and co-inventor of a patented frequency-hopping secret communication system later linked to modern wireless concepts.

trajectory.event: Starred in Ecstasy, gaining international fame and notoriety for its frank sexual content.
Fled marriage to Friedrich Mandl and met Louis B. Mayer, securing a path to Hollywood under the name Hedy Lamarr.
Hollywood breakthrough opposite Charles Boyer in Algiers; promoted by MGM as a major glamour star.
Co-starred in hit Boom Town with Clark Gable; solidified top-tier studio career before age 26.
U.S. patent 2,292,387 issued for Lamarr–Antheil frequency-hopping secret communication system.
Achieved her biggest commercial film success as Delilah in Samson and Delilah.
Received Electronic Frontier Foundation Pioneer Award with George Antheil for spread-spectrum contributions.
Died of heart disease in Florida; later inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame (2014).

name: Charles Kuta
milestone_by_age_26: In November 1981 at age ~25 he co-founded Silicon Graphics with James H. Clark and other Stanford colleagues; he contributed to the pipelined Geometry Engine for hardware 3D transforms.
early_history_summary: Raised in Pennsylvania; attended Atlantic College in Wales, then earned a first-class engineering science degree at University College, Oxford (1974–1977). Pursued a master's at Stanford and was recruited into the founding team of SGI around Clark's Geometry Engine work, launching one of the defining 1980s graphics workstation companies.
primary_leverage_engine: Scarce technical depth in graphics hardware/software
secondary_engine: Elite Stanford research ecosystem and complementary founding team
family_context_summary: Brought up in Pennsylvania; family financial and parental domain details not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Oxford first-class degree, Stanford master's, Jim Clark Geometry Engine circle, SGI founding team
evidence_summary: Wikipedia and Silicon Graphics corporate histories place Kuta as a 1956-born co-founder with Clark et al.; SGI was founded November 9, 1981, when he was about 25. Oxford first-class engineering science and Stanford graduate study put him in the Geometry Engine cohort. Later roles at Pellucid, Quantum3D, Palm, and CrowdStrike continue a graphics/systems engineering trajectory. Family background is sparsely documented.
starting_point: Born 1956 in Pennsylvania; international secondary path via Atlantic College (Wales) then University College, Oxford engineering science.
current_position: Living electronics/software engineer and SGI co-founder; later Quantum3D co-founder and engineer at Palm and CrowdStrike (public profile still active mid-2020s).

trajectory.event: Earned a first-class engineering science degree at University College, Oxford after studies from 1974–1977.
Co-founded Silicon Graphics with James Clark and Stanford colleagues; worked on Geometry Engine hardware for 3D transforms.
Co-founded Quantum3D and served as VP of System Software Architecture after prior work at Pellucid.
Continued systems/software engineering leadership roles including later work at Palm, Inc.
Associated with later security/engineering work including CrowdStrike in public bios.

name: Zach Perret
milestone_by_age_26: In late 2012 / early 2013 at age 25 he co-founded Plaid with William Hockey (after Bain 2010–2012), starting the fintech API company that became critical banking infrastructure.
early_history_summary: Raised in small-town North Carolina (Winston-Salem area); studied chemistry/biology (and physics per some bios) at Duke, then joined Bain as a junior associate where he met co-founder William Hockey. They first tried consumer budgeting apps, then pivoted to a developer banking API after hitting bank-connectivity friction.
primary_leverage_engine: Product/domain insight into bank connectivity friction
secondary_engine: Complementary cofounder + fintech API structural wave
family_context_summary: Grew up in small-town North Carolina; detailed parental occupations and wealth not documented in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented as a banking/fintech family path.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Duke, Bain peer Hockey, bank-API pivot, early fintech wave
evidence_summary: IMDb lists birth date September 17, 1987; Wikipedia/Forbes/TechCrunch agree he co-founded Plaid with Hockey after Bain, with founding activity 2012–2013 (age 25). Pivot from consumer finance tools to a unified banking API is well documented. Later Plaid scaled into major fintech infrastructure (Visa attempted acquisition; multi-billion valuation). Family background is lightly documented; cofounder trust and early fintech demand are primary accelerators.
starting_point: Born September 17, 1987; raised in small-town North Carolina and educated at Duke University before Bain consulting.
current_position: Co-founder and CEO of Plaid; major fintech infrastructure company; Forbes has listed him among self-made fintech billionaires in prior years; based in San Francisco.

trajectory.event: Joined Bain & Company as an associate after Duke; met future cofounder William Hockey.
Left Bain and co-founded what became Plaid, initially building consumer finance tools.
Pivoted Plaid toward a developer banking API and began early investor/customer traction (including NEA interest).
Raised early institutional capital as Plaid's bank-connectivity API gained developer adoption.
Visa announced a planned ~$5.3B acquisition of Plaid (later abandoned after DOJ challenge).
Plaid continued as independent fintech infrastructure after the Visa deal collapsed; Hockey later stepped back.
Remains CEO of Plaid as the company continues fundraising and product expansion in payments and data.
